deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from pp. 53-54): p = 4q+1 is prime. R = {1, alpha, beta, gamma, ...} is the set of n distinct residues of fourth powers mod p. R is closed under multiplication and division mod p. x is a non-residue whose square x^2 is also a non-residue. Euler forms the classes I = xR, II = x^2R, III = x^3R. Each has n elements, the classes are pairwise disjoint (§428), and x^4 lies in R. So the number of non-residues is at least 3n, and 4n <= 4q. If the three classes exhaust the non-residues, then n = q (§429). Since II together with R is exactly the set of squares lying in II u R, it suffices to show that every square non-residue lies in II (§§431-433). For contradiction, Euler supposes a square non-residue y^2 not in II, giving classes IV = yR, V = y^2R, VI = y^3R (§434). In §435 xy cannot be a residue: xy in R would force y in x^{-1}R = x^3R = III.

§436. Assume the six classes exhaust the non-residues, so the non-residue xy lies in one of them. Cancelling mod p (my explicit steps):
- xy = alpha x gives y = alpha, a residue.
- xy = alpha x^2 gives y = alpha x, in I.
- xy = alpha x^3 gives y = alpha x^2, in II.
- xy = alpha y gives x in R.
- xy = alpha y^2 gives x in IV.
- xy = alpha y^3 gives x in V.
All six contradict the disjointness of the classes. So six classes are impossible.

§437. Hence there are either exactly three classes or more than six. The latter happens if some square non-residue z^2 lies in neither II nor V. This gives classes VII = zR, VIII = z^2R, IX = z^3R, each with n terms.

§438. As in §435, none of xy, xz, yz is a residue. As in §436, xy is not in classes I-VI, so it must lie in VII-IX. Euler examines only the case xy = alpha z.

§439. If xy = alpha z, Euler asserts that the non-residue xz must equal beta y^nu with nu in {1,2,3}. This is implicitly justified by the analogue of §436 for the pairs (x,z) and nine exhaustive classes. Then
 z(xy - alpha z) - y(xz - beta y^nu) = beta y^(nu+1) - alpha z^2 = 0 mod p.
So z^2 would lie in y^(nu+1)R:
- nu = 3: z^2 in R, a contradiction.
- nu = 1: z^2 in V, contrary to the choice of z.
- nu = 2: z^2 in VI, also impossible. Euler just says 'in another class'. My filled step: squaring gives z^4 in y^6R = y^2R, so y^2 would be in R.

§440. Conclusion claimed: for prime p = 4q+1 there are exactly q distinct biquadratic residues, and the non-residues fall into three classes of q each.

§441. The 2q fourth powers 1^4, ..., (2q)^4 take only q distinct values, and each value is attained twice. So for each a <= 2q there is a unique b <= 2q, b != a, with p | b^4 - a^4. (Uniqueness is really supplied by §444.)

§442. b^4 - a^4 = (b-a)(b+a)(b^2+a^2). Here 0 < |b-a| and b+a <= 4q-1 < p, so p | a^2+b^2. Thus for every prime p = 4q+1 and every a in [1,2q] there is b in [1,2q] with p | a^2+b^2. This is equivalent to -1 being a quadratic residue mod p.

§443. Recall: a sum of two coprime squares has no odd prime divisors except those of the form 4n+1. Euler says it 'seems' to follow that every prime 4q+1 is a sum of two squares. What is certain: some multiple m*p (m = 1, 2, 5, 13, ...) is a sum of two squares. Indeed a^2+b^2 <= 8q^2 < 2q*p, so m < 2q. The descent completing the two-squares theorem is not given here.

§444. Independent proof that no three of a, b, c <= 2q have equal fourth powers mod p. By §442, p would divide a^2+b^2, a^2+c^2 and b^2+c^2, hence also the differences, e.g. a^2-c^2 = (a-c)(a+c). But 0 < |a-c| < p and 0 < a+c < p, so this is impossible. Hence each fourth-power value is hit at most twice in [1,2q], so n >= q. Combined with n <= q from §429, this gives n = q. Unlike §§436-439, this argument is sound (cf. §445 'nova ratione').
errors: §§436-439 use only group-theoretic properties (cosets of R in a quotient group of exponent 4) and never a field-specific fact. A non-cyclic quotient such as Z4 x Z4 satisfies every property invoked, so the argument cannot be complete.

§439: the concrete gap is the assertion that xz must lie in a y-class. Nothing justifies this unless one assumes the nine classes exhaust the non-residues. Even then, larger configurations (12, 15, ... classes) are not treated.
§438-439 treat only xy = alpha z. The cases xy = alpha z^2 and xy = alpha z^3 are omitted. They can be handled similarly, e.g. alpha z^3 = beta y^(nu+1) forces z in R, z^2 in R, or z in IV.
§439: in the case nu = 2, the disjointness of VIII from VI is asserted ('in alia classe'), not proved. It is provable: squaring gives y^2 in R.
§436 tacitly relies on the pairwise disjointness of all six classes; disjointness between the x-classes and the y-classes was only argued implicitly.

§441: 'a numerus quicunque minor quam 2q' should read 'non major quam 2q', since a = 2q is allowed. Also, the uniqueness of b does not follow from counting alone; it needs §444 (or the bound of at most 4 roots).

§443: Euler explicitly flags the passage to 'every prime 4q+1 is a sum of two squares' as only apparent ('concludi posse videtur'). The descent step is missing. The list 2, 5, 13 etc. of possible multipliers m omits m = 1 and is only illustrative.

results.what: For prime p = 4q+1 the fourth-power residues number q, and the non-residues form three cosets x R, x^2 R, x^3 R
results.modern_name: Index of the subgroup of fourth powers in (Z/pZ)^* is gcd(4, p-1) = 4; the quotient is cyclic of order 4
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (power-residue papers, e.g. E262, 1760s); later systematized by Gauss, Disquisitiones (1801)

results.what: For p = 4q+1 prime and any a <= 2q there is b <= 2q with p | a^2 + b^2, obtained via b^4 = a^4 mod p and factoring b^4 - a^4
results.modern_name: -1 is a quadratic residue mod p for p = 1 mod 4 (first supplement to quadratic reciprocity)
results.usually_credited_to: Fermat (statement); Euler (proofs, 1747-1750 letters to Goldbach, E241)

results.what: Some multiple m*p with m < 2q is a sum of two squares; conjecturally p itself is
results.modern_name: Fermat's two-squares theorem (preliminary step of descent)

results.what: No three of 1..2q have congruent fourth powers mod p, giving a second proof that n = q
results.modern_name: x^4 = c has at most 4 solutions mod p (Lagrange's polynomial congruence theorem, special case)
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1768) in general; Euler for special cases

deep.surprise_reason: The page is part of Euler's Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792), published in 1849 and well known. Biquadratic residue counts and -1 being a QR mod 4q+1 are standard Euler material. The only notable features are a flawed group-theoretic proof attempt and Euler's own hedging on the two-squares conclusion.

checkable.asserts: Exactly q distinct biquadratic residues mod p = 4q+1 (§440)
For each a <= 2q there is exactly one other b <= 2q with b^4 = a^4 mod p (§441, §444)
Such a pair satisfies p | a^2 + b^2 (§442)
The multiplier m in a^2+b^2 = m*p satisfies m < 2q (§443)

transcription_corrections: No substantive discrepancies found; the transcription matches the printed page (the § sign in §438 and the exponents y^(nu+1) and 16q^4 = (2q)^4 are read correctly).
